claims.text: Unmodified TC4 is an alpha-plus-beta dual-phase alloy.
Unmodified TC4 has relatively low surface hardness.
Unmodified TC4 has poor friction and wear properties.
TiAl-based coatings with varying Ni content have been laser-clad onto TC4 and evaluated for hardness and wear resistance.
Minor Ni additions promote formation of intermetallic compounds in the proposed coating.
The laser-clad layer will contain Fe2Ti, Ni3Ti, and Co2Ti intermetallic phases.
Laser cladding will produce a refined coating microstructure.
The refined microstructure will enhance dislocation-barrier effects.
Rapid solidification during laser cladding causes in-situ formation of intermetallic phases.
Solid-solution strengthening in a laser-clad TiAl coating is proposed to improve the wear resistance of TC4.
Hard intermetallic phases and solid-solution strengthening will increase surface hardness and wear resistance.
The coating will maintain good metallurgical bonding with the TC4 substrate.
The coating will increase TC4 surface hardness to approximately 1.5–2 times that of untreated TC4.
The coating will significantly reduce wear rate relative to untreated TC4.
Applying the coating will preserve TC4's high strength-to-weight ratio.
Applying the coating will preserve TC4's corrosion resistance.
The expected improvement applies under ambient sliding-wear conditions.
The coating is expected to perform under moderate-to-high contact stresses representative of aerospace and biomedical service.
Long-term adhesion and performance under extreme cyclic loading or high temperature have not been established.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% hardness increase and a 15% wear-rate reduction, or failure to detect the intended phases, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated coating chemistry identifies TiAl and optional Ni, but the mediator predicts Fe2Ti and Co2Ti without specifying any Fe or Co source.

The predicted hardness increase is 50–100%, whereas the falsification rule accepts any increase of at least 20%; an observed 20–49% increase would contradict the quantitative prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
